summary:
NW Rota-1 is an active submarine volcano 64 km northwest of Rota in the Mariana Islands. Its summit lies 517 m below sea level, and its active crater, Brimstone Pit, has provided the first direct observations of explosive eruptions underwater, beginning in 2004.

Eruptions observed from 2004 to 2010 included bursts of ash and gas, lava emission and Strombolian-style explosions. Activity shifted among vents, and hydrophones recorded repeated acoustic bursts. On 14 August 2009, a major landslide stripped part of the volcano’s southern flank, generating an underwater ash plume. The volcano was acoustically quiet for a time afterward. A 2014 ROV dive found no activity.

Hydrothermal vents release sulfur, carbon dioxide and other compounds. Estimated carbon dioxide emissions are 400,000 ± 100,000 tonnes annually. Microbial mats support shrimp, crabs and other animals, but eruptions and landslides limit animal diversity. The seamount is part of the Mariana volcanic arc and the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument.
